caption:
Did tulip bulbs really sell for the price of a house?

Some did. At the peak, in February 1637, certain bulbs traded for more than ten times the annual income of a skilled artisan. A Viceroy tulip was worth upwards of five times the cost of an average house. The Semper Augustus, the most expensive of all, sold for ƒ10,000 — about €130,000 in 2024 money.

The flames and stripes that made those bulbs precious were a disease: a tulip-specific mosaic virus that "breaks" one petal colour into two. It also progressively impairs the bulb's production of daughter bulbs.

Almost no bulbs moved. Traders met in tavern "colleges", signed forward contracts, paid 2.5% wine money, and called the whole business windhandel — air trade. In February 1637 buyers stopped turning up. Prices collapsed inside a week, and most contracts were simply never honoured.

Charles Mackay's Extraordinary Popular Delusions (1841) turned it into a nation ruined. Since the 1980s economists have debunked much of that. Anne Goldgar's archive work found the trade was conducted almost entirely by wealthy merchants and craftsmen, and that fewer than half a dozen of them ran into financial trouble — and even then, tulips may not be to blame.

Still open: the actual circumstances of the crash are unknown, and economists argue whether this was a bubble at all. Earl Thompson argued the prices were tracking a coming change in contract law.

Images: a Semper Augustus watercolour, before 1640; a plate from P. Cos's 1637 tulip catalogue; the Alkmaar auction price list of 5 February 1637; the pamphlet Tooneel van Flora, Amsterdam 1637; Hendrik Gerritsz Pot's Flora's Wagon of Fools, c.1637; and Jan Brueghel the Younger's monkey allegory. All public domain.
